prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My desk is cleared of the litter of ages; Before me glitter the fair white pages; My fountain pen is clean and filled, And the noise of the office has long been stilled. Roget’s Thesaurus is at my hand, And I’m ready to do some work that’s grand, Dignified, eminent, great, momentous, Memorable, worthy of note, portentous, Beautiful, paramount, vital, prime, Stirring, eventful, august, sublime. For this is the way, I have read and heard, That authors look for the fitting word. All of the proud ingredients mine To build, like Marlowe, the mighty line. But never a line from my new-filled pen That couldn’t be done by a child of ten. Oh, how did Shelley and how did Keats Weave magic words on the fair white sheets Under conditions that, were they mine, I couldn’t bear? And I’d just resign. Yet Milton wrote passable literature Under conditions I couldn’t endure. Coleridge and Chatterton did their stuff Over a road that I’d christen rough. Wordsworth and—soft!—could it be that they Waited until they had something to say?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Before, And, Roget

outputs.L1:
# Polished Version

My desk stands cleared of accumulated clutter;
Before me, pristine white pages glimmer.
My fountain pen sits clean and filled,
And the office's clamor has long since stilled.

Roget's Thesaurus rests within reach,
And I'm prepared to craft something magnificent—
Dignified, eminent, momentous, grand,
Memorable, noteworthy, portentous work at hand,
Beautiful, paramount, vital, sublime,
Stirring, eventful, august in design.

For this, I've read and understood,
Is how true authors seek the perfect word.
All these noble ingredients are mine
To forge, like Marlowe, the mighty line.

Yet never a line from my freshly-filled pen
Surpasses what any child of ten might pen.
Oh, how did Shelley, how did Keats,
Weave such enchantment across their sheets,
Under conditions that, were they my own,
I could not bear—I'd simply be gone?

Yet Milton composed enduring literature
Amid hardships I could scarcely endure.
Coleridge and Chatterton pursued their art
Along a road I'd deem rough from the start.

Wordsworth and—wait—could it perhaps be
That they waited until they had something to say?

---

*Note: I've preserved the poem's rhyme scheme, rhythm, and all original content while refining word choices and flow for greater elegance. The self-deprecating wit and central irony—that despite having every literary "tool" at hand, true inspiration cannot be manufactured—remains intact.*

outputs.L3:
# The Illusion of the Perfect Writing Conditions

The speaker begins with a ritual familiar to many aspiring writers: he meticulously prepares his workspace, clearing his desk until it gleams, selecting a fresh pen that glides smoothly across the page, and ensuring his office is enveloped in silence, free from any distraction. To complete this seemingly perfect setup, he arms himself with a thesaurus, hoping to pepper his writing with grandiose, sophisticated vocabulary that might lend his words an air of literary greatness.

Yet despite assembling all these "proud ingredients"—the clean desk, the quiet room, the impressive lexicon—the speaker arrives at a humbling and somewhat comedic realization: his writing, for all this preparation, is no more accomplished than something a child might scrawl in a notebook. The elaborate setup has yielded nothing extraordinary, exposing the gap between external conditions and genuine literary merit.

This failure prompts the speaker to reflect on the great poets of history—Shelley, Keats, and Milton—who produced timeless, masterful works despite enduring circumstances far harsher than his own. These writers faced poverty, illness, blindness, and personal turmoil, conditions the speaker admits he could scarcely tolerate, let alone create under. Their brilliance emerged not from comfort but often in spite of profound adversity.

The speaker extends this observation to Coleridge and Chatterton, further examples of literary figures who achieved greatness while traveling what he calls a "rough road" of hardship, struggle, and suffering. Their success seems to defy the very premise that ideal conditions are necessary for great art—suggesting instead that genius can flourish, and perhaps even sharpen, amid difficulty.

The poem concludes with a wry, ironic twist: perhaps the true secret of writers like Wordsworth wasn't their environment or their vocabulary at all, but simply patience—the wisdom to wait until they actually had something meaningful to say. Rather than forcing profundity through elaborate rituals or borrowed grandiloquence, perhaps these poets understood that authentic inspiration cannot be manufactured through a clean desk or a well-thumbed thesaurus, but must arise organically, when genuine insight and emotion finally converge.
outputs.L4:
# The Poet's Dilemma

I cleared my desk of clutter,
swept away the crumbs and dust,
arranged my papers in neat piles
as any serious writer must.

I filled my pen with ink so black,
tested it on scrap paper first,
made sure the nib would glide just right
before I let my genius burst.

I opened up the thesaurus thick,
searched for words both grand and rare—
"effulgent," "sempiternal," "sublime"—
surely greatness needs such flair!

I sat up straight, I cleared my throat,
I struck a pose both wise and keen,
I waited for the muse to strike
and paint my page with words pristine.

But nothing came. The page stayed blank.
My grand words sat there, cold and dead.
No flash of brilliance, no spark of fire—
just silence echoing in my head.

So I began to wonder then
about the poets I revered:
Did Shelley have a tidy desk?
Did Keats wait till his ink appeared?

Poor Keats, they say, wrote feverish lines
while tuberculosis claimed his breath,
no time for thesaurus-hunting words—
he raced instead against his death.

And Shelley, drowned before his time,
wrote wild and stormy, quick and true,
not pausing once to check if "azure"
sounded better than plain "blue."

Milton, blind, could not have seen
the words he chose upon the page—
he dictated Paradise, every line,
from darkness, not some lighted stage.

And Coleridge, dreaming opium dreams,
woke up and simply let it flow—
no perfect pen, no polished desk,
just visions demanding somewhere to go.

So here I sit with all my tools,
my sharpened pen, my thesaurus new,
my perfect desk, my perfect chair—
and not one word that rings as true.

Perhaps the secret isn't in
the proper setup, clean and neat,
but something burning in the chest
that makes the pen and paper meet.

Perhaps it's not the fancy words
or comfort found in tidy rooms—
perhaps it's simply having something
worth the saying, which consumes.

So I'll set aside my empty tricks,
my hollow search for words that dazzle,
and wait instead for something real—
some truth, some fire, some genuine hassle.

For all the tools mean nothing much
without a reason to pick up the pen,
and all the greats knew one true thing:
you write because you must—not when
the desk is clean, the ink runs smooth,
the thesaurus lies open, primed—
but when you have something to say
that's worth the trouble to be rhymed.
outputs.L5:
# Before and Roget: A Reflection on Finding Words

Before Roget, there was only the frustration of the tip-of-the-tongue moment—that maddening sensation of knowing precisely what you mean but lacking the exact word to express it. Before Roget, writers and speakers relied on memory, intuition, and the limited vocabulary that happened to surface in the moment of need.

And then, in 1852, Peter Mark Roget changed this experience forever with the publication of his *Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases*. A physician by training and a man of remarkably diverse interests, Roget approached language with the same systematic mind he brought to science. He didn't simply alphabetize synonyms; he organized concepts into categories, creating a taxonomy of meaning that mirrored the way ideas naturally cluster in human thought.

Before Roget's innovation, dictionaries told you what words meant. And Roget's thesaurus told you what words *related* to what you already knew—it started with the concept and worked outward to the vocabulary, rather than starting with a word and working toward definition.

The genius of Roget's approach lay in its recognition that language isn't merely a list of labels but a web of interconnected ideas. Words like "happy," "joyful," "content," and "elated" aren't just synonyms—they're points along a spectrum of meaning, each carrying subtle shades of intensity, connotation, and context.

Before Roget, writers searched. And after Roget, they discovered. The thesaurus became not just a reference tool but a creative instrument, helping generations of writers, students, and thinkers locate the precise word that had been hovering just beyond reach—transforming vague impressions into sharp, specific expression.

Today, whether consulted in print or embedded invisibly within our word processors, Roget's legacy persists: the simple but profound idea that finding the right word is really about understanding the landscape of ideas that word belongs to.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous poem about a writer sitting down at a clean desk with a thesaurus, trying to write something profound but only producing mediocre lines, ending with a witty observation about famous poets.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Thesaurus Betrayal

I sat me down at desk so clean,
The tidiest that I'd yet seen,
With pen in hand and mind so keen,
To write the Greatest Words Yet Seen.

I cracked my thesaurus with glee—
"I'll find the perfect word!" said me.
"Not 'happy,' no—I'll write 'ebullient'!"
My sentence now sounds... somewhat truculent.

"The moon," I wrote, "hung there, resplendent,"
Then changed to "lunar-esque, transcendent,"
Then panicked, crossed it out in shame,
And wrote "the moon was round" again.

I sought a word for "very sad"
And found "lugubrious"—not bad!
But stuffed in every line I had,
Until my poem sounded mad:

*"My lugubrious heart, ebullient-broken,
Speaks words that transcendental-esque have spoken,
In verdant sorrow, resplendently woken—"*
(This metaphor, I fear, is smoken.)

Three hours passed. My coffee's cold.
My "profound truths" grow thin and old.
I've used "cerulean" for "blue"
Four times—which even *I* thought was too... much.

So here's my witty final thought,
The wisdom that this morning bought:
Shakespeare didn't need a thesaurus—
He just made up the words *before* us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you compose a witty, old-fashioned verse about writer's block, where the poet mocks their own attempts at greatness by comparing themselves to Shelley, Keats, Milton, and Wordsworth?
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Affliction of a Barren Muse

I sat me down to write a verse of towering, grand design,
To pen the sort of deathless words that echo down through time—
I dipped my quill with Shelley's fire ablaze within my breast,
And stared at empty parchment for the better part of a rest.

"Surely," quoth I to myself, "I've got the poet's gift!
Like Keats, I'll craft an ode so sweet it sets the soul adrift!"
But all that came from mine own pen, when put unto the test,
Was: *"Roses red, the sky is blue, I really must digest."*

Then Milton's ghost, I did invoke, to help me reach the skies,
To justify the ways of verse to critical, sharp eyes—
Twelve books he wrote of Paradise, both lost and then regained;
I wrote twelve lines about my tea and how the cup was stained.

I turned at last to Wordsworth's craft, so humble and sublime,
Who found in daffodils and clouds a wealth of thought and rhyme—
I wandered lonely as a cloud (or was it just a fool?),
And found not inspiration, but a puddle, dark and cool.

So here's to all the mighty bards whose names shall never fade,
While I shall be remembered as the one who never made
A single verse worth reading, save this mock and sorry rhyme
That proves, at least, I tried my best to kill a bit of time.

For genius, I have come to know, cannot be forced or bought—
It seems the Muse has left the house and won't return, methought.
So I shall raise a toast to Keats, to Shelley, and the rest,
And go to bed admitting that mediocrity's my best.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem in the style of early 20th-century light verse about an author preparing to write a masterpiece but only managing childish lines, with a punchline about needing something to actually say.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE GREAT AMERICAN NOTHING**

I sharpened seven pencils to a point precise and fine,
I settled in my study with the clock struck half-past nine,
I smoothed a virgin tablet on the blotter, crisp and white,
And thought, "Tonight's the night I write the Novel of the Night."

I flexed my wrist. I cracked my knuckles. I assumed the pose
Of Genius Deep in Thought, as every frontispiece photo shows.
I murmured, "Call me Ishmael"—no, that line's been used before.
I tried, "It was the best of times"—alas, a fellow's done that too, what's more.

I chewed my pencil thoughtfully. I stared into the middle space.
I furrowed up my noble brow in a most Homeric grimace.
Then, seized at last by inspiration's fierce and fiery dart,
I wrote: **"The cat sat on the mat."**
That was the whole of Art.

I read it over, rather pleased—the meter, clean and terse,
Yet something nagged... a small suspicion... was it possibly worse?
I added, boldly: **"Then it got up. The cat, I mean. And walked away."**
The masterpiece was taking shape! Or so I longed to say.

I wrote three hours, filled six pages, sweated through my shirt,
Produced a saga of a cat who mostly sat, then stirred.
No plot arrived. No theme took root. No character grew wise.
Just cats, and mats, and sitting, viewed from seventeen different eyes.

So here's my grand confession, offered humbly, plain, and flat:
I've got the desk. I've got the pen. I've even got the cat.
I've got the whole equipment of Literature's proud array—

I just don't have a **blessed thing** that I've got to say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a comic poem about the gap between having the right writing tools (thesaurus, pen, quiet office) and actual talent, referencing classic poets like Marlowe, Coleridge, and Wordsworth.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Well-Equipped Amateur

I bought myself a fountain pen
of burnished gold and jet,
a thesaurus thick as Sunday roast,
the finest Moleskine yet.

I built a study lined with oak,
hung portraits on the wall—
Marlowe smirking, quill in hand,
who wrote "Come live with me" and all
those lines that made the shepherds sing
and maidens swoon for love,
while I sat staring at blank pages,
mittens on, in my office (heated, above).

I lit a candle, "for the mood,"
and read some Coleridge aloud—
that fellow dreamed of Xanadu
on opium, uncrowned,
while I had *ambiance diffusers*
and a chair from Herman Miller,
yet nothing flowed but my frustration
and a half-eaten thriller.

I thought of Wordsworth on his walks,
communing with the trees,
who needed just a daffodil
to bring him to his knees
with feeling—I have hiking boots,
a Fitbit, and a drone
to film my "nature moments,"
yet I wander, muse-alone.

My thesaurus offers me "effulgent"
when I mean to just say "bright."
My pen glides smooth as poetry
but writes: *"the sky was, like, so white."*
I've got the desk. I've got the lamp.
I've got the vintage quill.
What I don't have—turns out—
is any actual skill.

So here's to you, you tortured greats,
who wrote with wounds, not wealth,
who needed nothing but a scrap
and something dark in themselves—
while I sit here, my office pristine,
my tools all shined and true,
producing garbage, elegantly—
at least my desk looks like yours *do*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a satirical poem about a writer who sets up the perfect conditions to write something 'grand' and 'sublime,' but ends up realizing the real secret of great poets was having actual content to express.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Sublime Conditions**

He bought the candles—beeswax, hand-poured, dim,
the kind that Keats might plausibly have burned.
He cleared his desk of everything but him
and one blank page, expensive, cream, unlearned.

He brewed a tea that Coleridge once described
(imported, bitter, faintly opium-laced).
He read that Whitman wrote his lines outside,
so he dragged his desk into the yard, disgraced

the neighbor's view with his dramatic pose.
He wore a shirt with billowing white sleeves.
He lit some incense, struck a pensive nose-
to-sky position that a genius achieves

right before greatness. Waited. Waited more.
The candle guttered. Tea went cold and gray.
He'd read that Yeats communed with ancient lore
through spirits speaking in an automatic way,

so he tried that too—closed eyes, went slack,
invited ghosts to scribble through his hand.
Nothing arrived. He tried a different tack:
he researched *sublime* until he'd planned

the perfect storm of soul-appropriate weather—
a storm, in fact, would help, so he checked the sky,
found only sun, and cursed his luck. Together,
the candles, tea, the shirt, the reasons why

great men wrote great things sat there, all correct,
all borrowed, primed, importuned, and precise—
except the thing itself. He'd quite forget
that Whitman wrote of *something*—wars, and lice,

and bodies, love, the smell of grass at dawn—
not just the desk he happened to be seated at.
That Keats wrote nightingales because they'd gone
and sung to him, not because he sat and sat

waiting for a nightingale's *idea*
to strike him like a coach strikes a stray dog.
He blew the candles out. The atmosphere
dissolved to what it was: a man, a fog

of his own making, and a page as blank
as when he'd started, hours of ritual spent
buying the *feeling* while the meaning sank
beneath the pageantry of ornament.

He'd built a temple with no god to house.
He'd set the perfect table, empty-served.
The secret wasn't tea, or shirt, or blouse
of incense-smoke—it's that the greats observed

something *worth saying*, then sat down to say it,
plainly, urgently, however dressed.
He had no news to tell and tried to weigh it
in silver settings, hoping for the best.

He put the candles back. He drank his coffee black.
He wrote about a man who tried too hard—
and there, at last, arriving from the lack
of anything but *this*, he found his card:

not sublime conditions, robes, or myth,
but one true thing he actually meant.
He wrote it down. It wasn't much. But with
that plainness came the first real element.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
